subject: Astronomy & Space
title: Betelgeuse: The Shoulder of Orion
description: A quick win: understand Betelgeuse: The Shoulder of Orion.

hook.text: Betelgeuse is a red supergiant so large that if it replaced the Sun, it would engulf Mars.

buildup.text: It sits on Orion's shoulder, glowing reddish-orange and visibly pulsing as it expands and contracts.

discovery.text: In 2019, Betelgeuse suddenly dimmed by 35%. Astronomers wondered if it was about to explode.

twist.text: It turned out a giant dust cloud had blocked our view. Betelgeuse hadn't changed—just hidden itself.

climax.text: When it does explode, it will shine brighter than the full Moon for weeks—visible even in daylight.

punchline.text: A dying giant on Orion's shoulder. The explosion could come any millennium.

quiz.question: What caused Betelgeuse's dramatic dimming in 2019?
options: A giant cloud of dust it ejected temporarily blocked our view
The star began collapsing before an imminent supernova
A companion star passed in front of it

details.summary: Betelgeuse is a red supergiant star marking Orion's shoulder, about 700 light-years away. It's roughly 1,000 times the Sun's diameter and nearing the end of its life — destined to explode as a supernova within the next 100,000 years.
details.whyItMatters: Betelgeuse is the nearest red supergiant and a prime candidate for the next visible supernova. Its explosion would be visible in daylight and cast shadows at night — the most spectacular astronomical event in recorded history.
takeaways: Betelgeuse is a red supergiant about 1,000 times the Sun's size
It will explode as a supernova within 100,000 years
Its 2019-2020 dimming sparked widespread supernova speculation

faq.question: What caused the Great Dimming of 2019-2020?
faq.answer: Betelgeuse ejected a massive cloud of dust from its surface that partially blocked our view, combined with a natural pulsation cycle that dimmed the star. It was not a supernova precursor. The dimming was the most dramatic observed change in a bright star in modern astronomy.

faq.question: Would Betelgeuse's supernova be dangerous to Earth?
faq.answer: No. At 700 light-years away, it's too distant to cause harm. It would be visible in daylight for weeks and at night for months, roughly as bright as the full moon. It would be spectacular but harmless — supernovae need to be within about 50 light-years to threaten Earth.
